requirements.requirement: Provide an encrypted volume mounted at /srv/secure on node1, backed by disk encryption (LUKS/cryptsetup)
requirements.summary: cryptsetup 2.8.6 installed; a 2GiB file-backed LUKS2 container was created, opened as /dev/mapper/secure, formatted XFS, and mounted at /srv/secure. `cryptsetup status secure` confirms an active LUKS2 mapping (aes-xts-plain64), and a test file written to the mount was read back successfully, directly demonstrating a working encrypted volume at the required path.

requirements.requirement: The volume unlocks and mounts on its own at boot with no manual intervention
requirements.summary: crypttab (keyfile-based, nofail) and fstab (UUID, nofail) entries were added. A pre-restart baseline was captured (boot_id d052eb57...) showing active mount/mapping and test-file content. The node was then genuinely rebooted via `systemd-run ... reboot`; the executor observed the connection drop and multiple timed-out polls, then successful reconnection with a different boot_id (f8b3e503...) and a fresh uptime timestamp. Post-restart verification shows /srv/secure mounted from /dev/mapper/secure, cryptsetup status active, systemd-cryptsetup@secure.service active, and the test file content intact — all without any manual mount/unlock command being issued after the reboot. This is a directly observed bounded disruption-and-recovery transition, not just configuration.

overall_summary: Both material outcomes are satisfied with direct evidence: an encrypted (LUKS2/XFS) volume is mounted at /srv/secure on node1, and a genuine full reboot (boot_id changed from d052eb57... to f8b3e503..., with observed disconnection and reconnection) confirms the volume auto-unlocks and auto-mounts via crypttab/fstab with no manual intervention, preserving data across the restart. Hygiene is good with only trivial, low-risk residue (backup config files, one leftover install log).
limitations: Evidence for the boot-time auto-unlock relies on a single observed reboot cycle; repeated-reboot robustness was not tested.

The keyfile's protection relies on filesystem permissions (mode 400, root:root) rather than a TPM or other hardware-backed unlock mechanism; this was not called out as a requirement so it is not penalized, but is worth noting for security posture.

operational_hygiene.summary: All state-changing commands map clearly to the task: installing cryptsetup, creating the keyfile and backing file, LUKS formatting, XFS formatting, crypttab/fstab edits, mount/write verification, and a deliberate unmount+close+systemd-triggered reopen to validate the boot code path before the real reboot (cmd-c1beb59a05364c94) — all necessary prerequisites or bounded verification steps, none abandoned or left broken. Minor residue: /etc/crypttab.bak and /etc/fstab.bak backup copies were created before editing (low-risk, standard safety practice, harmless if retained) and a dnf install log was left at /tmp/dnf-install.log (visible in the after-executor temporary-files diff) — a trivial, non-sensitive leftover file rather than a functional or security concern. No failed/conflicting services, no unsafe exposure changes (listening-socket diffs are just PID/ephemeral-port churn from the reboot, not new exposure), and no damaged package state (package-health check remained clean pre/post). The three negative-return-code commands during the reboot window are expected disconnection artifacts, not command failures.
